newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK cheers China's MFN renewal as handover looms.
newsitem.headline: HK cheers China's MFN renewal as handover looms.

text.p: Hong Kong on Wednesday cheered a United States vote to renew China's trade privileges for another year as a powerful boost for the wealthy British colony six days before transfer to Chinese rule.

Hong Kong, a key economic and trading hub for East Asia, has always lobbied for the continuation of China's most favoured nation (MFN) trade status. The territory reverts to China on July 1 after 156 years of British colonialism.
The U.S. House of Representatives voted earlier by a sizeable margin of 259 to 173 to renew China's MFN status for another year, backing President Bill Clinton's decision.
Opponents of renewing MFN cite China's human rights record, copyright piracy, and allegations of transfer of missile technology and diverting U.S. technology to military purposes.
But Hong Kong argues that stopping China's MFN status would hurt the territory's economy more than Beijing's.

"We are very pleased with the result. The renewal of China's MFN status always matters greatly to Hong Kong, but it has never mattered more than this year when Hong Kong will embark on a new chapter in its history," the government said in a statement.
"The renewal...goes a long way to ensure the continued economic vibrancy of Hong Kong during the handover period."
Business leaders in Hong Kong also welcomed the decision.
"It's great news, the MFN season is always unpredictable," said Mitch Presnick, a partner with Warren Williams International Public Affairs Consultant.

The territory estimates it could lose up to US$30 billion annually in trade and related industry revenues if China lost its MFN status. Gross domestic product growth could be cut by about three percentage points and some 86,000 jobs lost.

The voting in the United States was closely watched after some conservatives and others in the House said they were preparing for a fight, pointing to China's policies on Hong Kong, human and religious rights, trade and other issues.
Some Hong Kong analysts said the large margin should open the way for Washington to stop the annual review and start considering granting China permanent trade privileges.

"The vote was overwhelmingly to support President Clinton in renewing China's MFN status. That should be the end of the annual MFN debate as a major exercise," said Bill Overholt, managing director of Asian research at Bankers Trust.
"This should really be the end, The debate now shifts to a debate over whether to grant permanent MFN," he said.
The American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, while happy about the outcome, said it would push for permanent MFN.
"Establishing regular trade status is the key to moving forwards in all aspects of the Sino-U.S. relationship," it said.
But the renewal did not appear extraordinary for some.
"I don't think there is any one person in Hong Kong who even questioned that China would not have its MFN status renewed," said Franklin Lam, director of research at SBC Warburg.
